claim: LRRK2 mutations produce end-stage Parkinson's disease (PD) with reduced nigrostriatal dopamine.
source: LRRK2 mutations produce end-stage Parkinson's disease (PD) with reduced nigrostriatal dopamine, whereas, asymptomatic carriers have increased dopamine turnover and altered brain connectivity.
evidence: This is a general statement about LRRK2 mutations in the abstract, drawing on established knowledge about PD pathology.

claim: Asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers have increased dopamine turnover.
source: LRRK2 mutations produce end-stage Parkinson's disease (PD) with reduced nigrostriatal dopamine, whereas, asymptomatic carriers have increased dopamine turnover and altered brain connectivity.
evidence: This statement references findings about asymptomatic carriers, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers have altered brain connectivity.
source: LRRK2 mutations produce end-stage Parkinson's disease (PD) with reduced nigrostriatal dopamine, whereas, asymptomatic carriers have increased dopamine turnover and altered brain connectivity.
evidence: This statement references findings about asymptomatic carriers, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Reduced dopamine and mitochondrial abnormalities occur in aged G2019S mutant knock-in (GKI) mice.
source: LRRK2 pathophysiology remains unclear, but reduced dopamine and mitochondrial abnormalities occur in aged G2019S mutant knock-in (GKI) mice.
evidence: This refers to previous findings in the GKI mouse model, supported by prior publications.

claim: Cultured GKI neurons exhibit increased synaptic transmission.
source: Conversely, cultured GKI neurons exhibit increased synaptic transmission.
evidence: This statement references prior experimental findings in cultured neurons from GKI mice.

claim: Young GKI mice exhibit more vertical exploration than wild-type littermates.
source: Young GKI mice exhibit more vertical exploration, elevated glutamate and dopamine transmission, and aberrant D2-receptor responses.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1B showing increased rearing events in young GKI mice.

claim: Young GKI mice exhibit elevated glutamate transmission.
source: Young GKI mice exhibit more vertical exploration, elevated glutamate and dopamine transmission, and aberrant D2-receptor responses.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2 showing increased sEPSC frequency in young GKI mice.

claim: Young GKI mice exhibit elevated dopamine transmission.
source: Young GKI mice exhibit more vertical exploration, elevated glutamate and dopamine transmission, and aberrant D2-receptor responses.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3 showing altered dopamine release dynamics in young GKI mice.

claim: Young GKI mice exhibit aberrant D2-receptor responses.
source: Young GKI mice exhibit more vertical exploration, elevated glutamate and dopamine transmission, and aberrant D2-receptor responses.
evidence: This is supported by data showing altered responses to quinpirole (D2 agonist) in young GKI mice in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Elevated glutamate and dopamine transmission decline with age in GKI mice.
source: These phenomena decline with age, but are stable in littermates.
evidence: This is supported by age-dependent comparisons in Figures 2 and 3 showing reductions in transmission measures in aged GKI mice.

claim: Glutamate and dopamine transmission are stable with age in wild-type littermates.
source: These phenomena decline with age, but are stable in littermates.
evidence: This is supported by age-dependent comparisons in Figures 2 and 3 showing stable transmission measures in aged WT mice.

claim: In young GKI mice, dopamine transients are slower than in wild-type mice.
source: In young GKI mice, dopamine transients are slower, independent of dopamine transporter (DAT), increasing the lifetime of extracellular dopamine.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3B showing increased decay times (Tau) in young GKI mice.

claim: Slowing of dopamine transients in young GKI mice is independent of dopamine transporter (DAT).
source: In young GKI mice, dopamine transients are slower, independent of dopamine transporter (DAT), increasing the lifetime of extracellular dopamine.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with DAT blocker GBR12909 showing persistent slowing in GKI mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Slower dopamine transients increase the lifetime of extracellular dopamine in young GKI mice.
source: In young GKI mice, dopamine transients are slower, independent of dopamine transporter (DAT), increasing the lifetime of extracellular dopamine.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the measured slower decay times of dopamine transients.

claim: Slowing of dopamine transients is observed with age in wild-type littermates.
source: Slowing of dopamine transients is observed with age in littermates, suggesting premature ageing of dopamine synapses in GKI mice.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3B showing increased decay times in aged WT mice.

claim: GKI mice exhibit premature ageing of dopamine synapses.
source: Slowing of dopamine transients is observed with age in littermates, suggesting premature ageing of dopamine synapses in GKI mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that young GKI mice show characteristics (slower transients) that appear in older WT mice.

claim: GKI mice exhibit early, but declining, synaptic and behavioral phenotypes.
source: Thus, GKI mice exhibit early, but declining, synaptic and behavioral phenotypes, making them amenable to investigation of early pathophysiological, and later parkinsonian-like, alterations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral and electrophysiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: GKI mice are amenable to investigation of early pathophysiological alterations.
source: Thus, GKI mice exhibit early, but declining, synaptic and behavioral phenotypes, making them amenable to investigation of early pathophysiological, and later parkinsonian-like, alterations.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the model based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: GKI mice are amenable to investigation of later parkinsonian-like alterations.
source: Thus, GKI mice exhibit early, but declining, synaptic and behavioral phenotypes, making them amenable to investigation of early pathophysiological, and later parkinsonian-like, alterations.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the model based on the observed phenotypes and prior findings.

claim: The GKI mouse model will prove valuable in efforts to develop neuroprotection for PD.
source: This model will prove valuable in efforts to develop neuroprotection for PD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the future utility of the model.

claim: Nigral cell death may be as low as 0–10% 1–3 years from PD diagnosis.
source: A recent study suggests nigral cell death may be as low as 0–10% 1–3 years from diagnosis, whereas dopamine functional markers such as tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine transporter (DAT) are profoundly reduced at the earliest points assessed (Kordower et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kordower et al., 2013.

claim: Dopamine functional markers such as tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine transporter (DAT) are profoundly reduced at the earliest points assessed in PD (1-3 years from diagnosis).
source: A recent study suggests nigral cell death may be as low as 0–10% 1–3 years from diagnosis, whereas dopamine functional markers such as tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine transporter (DAT) are profoundly reduced at the earliest points assessed (Kordower et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kordower et al., 2013.

claim: The rapid and near complete loss of dopamine functional markers at, or within a few years of, diagnosis argues that ongoing clinical deterioration over several years is due to loss of compensatory mechanisms and/or dysfunction of non-dopaminergic neurons.
source: The rapid and near complete loss of dopamine functional markers at, or within a few years of, diagnosis argues that ongoing clinical deterioration over several years is due to loss of compensatory mechanisms and/or dysfunction of non-dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings about dopamine markers and clinical progression.

claim: Motor symptoms in PD respond well to current therapy (e.g., dopamine replacement by L-DOPA or deep brain stimulation; DBS).
source: Although motor symptoms respond well to current therapy (e.g., dopamine replacement by L-DOPA or deep brain stimulation; DBS), PD is a multisystem disorder with a host of L-DOPA unresponsive features.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PD treatment.

claim: PD is a multisystem disorder with a host of L-DOPA unresponsive features.
source: Although motor symptoms respond well to current therapy (e.g., dopamine replacement by L-DOPA or deep brain stimulation; DBS), PD is a multisystem disorder with a host of L-DOPA unresponsive features.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PD.

claim: All PD patients suffer a range of non-motor symptoms.
source: All patients suffer a range of non-motor symptoms, many of which appear to precede motor onset by years or decades (Goldman and Postuma, 2014; Chaudhuri and Schapira, 2009; Jenner et al., 2013; Weintraub et al., 2008a, Weintraub et al., 2008b, Weintraub et al., 2008cWeintraub et al., 2008c; Tolosa et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many non-motor symptoms in PD appear to precede motor onset by years or decades.
source: All patients suffer a range of non-motor symptoms, many of which appear to precede motor onset by years or decades (Goldman and Postuma, 2014; Chaudhuri and Schapira, 2009; Jenner et al., 2013; Weintraub et al., 2008a, Weintraub et al., 2008b, Weintraub et al., 2008cWeintraub et al., 2008c; Tolosa et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cognitive dysfunction is seen in ~40% of newly diagnosed PD cases.
source: Cognitive dysfunction is seen in ~40% of newly diagnosed PD cases (Broeders et al., 2013; Pedersen et al., 2013; Litvan et al., 2011) in the form of deficits in attention, executive function, verbal fluency and visuospatial processing, rather than memory per se (although memory is also often impaired) (Weintraub et al., 2008b; Goldman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Cognitive dysfunction in newly diagnosed PD cases manifests as deficits in attention, executive function, verbal fluency and visuospatial processing, rather than memory per se.
source: Cognitive dysfunction is seen in ~40% of newly diagnosed PD cases (Broeders et al., 2013; Pedersen et al., 2013; Litvan et al., 2011) in the form of deficits in attention, executive function, verbal fluency and visuospatial processing, rather than memory per se (although memory is also often impaired) (Weintraub et al., 2008b; Goldman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Memory is also often impaired in newly diagnosed PD cases with cognitive dysfunction.
source: Cognitive dysfunction is seen in ~40% of newly diagnosed PD cases (Broeders et al., 2013; Pedersen et al., 2013; Litvan et al., 2011) in the form of deficits in attention, executive function, verbal fluency and visuospatial processing, rather than memory per se (although memory is also often impaired) (Weintraub et al., 2008b; Goldman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The dysexecutive/subcortical syndrome in PD is thought to be due to impaired cortico-striatal basal ganglia processing for action selection.
source: This dysexecutive/subcortical syndrome is thought to be due to impaired cortico-striatal basal ganglia processing for action selection (Goldman and Postuma, 2014; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: There are no effective symptomatic treatments for many non-motor issues in PD.
source: There are no effective symptomatic treatments for many of these non-motor issues, nor are there currently any disease-modifying (neuroprotective) interventions.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PD treatment limitations.

claim: There are currently no disease-modifying (neuroprotective) interventions for PD.
source: There are no effective symptomatic treatments for many of these non-motor issues, nor are there currently any disease-modifying (neuroprotective) interventions.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PD treatment limitations.

claim: Gene mutations contribute the most risk for PD, aside from age.
source: While the etiology for most Parkinson patients remains unknown, aside from age, gene mutations contribute the most risk (Volta et al., 2015a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: Pathogenic mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) account for ~1% of all PD cases.
source: Pathogenic mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) account for ~1% of all PD cases, of which LRRK2 G2019S is the most frequent; identified in ~30% of cases in some ethnicities (Ozelius et al., 2006; Hulihan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: LRRK2 G2019S is the most frequent LRRK2 mutation.
source: Pathogenic mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) account for ~1% of all PD cases, of which LRRK2 G2019S is the most frequent; identified in ~30% of cases in some ethnicities (Ozelius et al., 2006; Hulihan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: LRRK2 G2019S is identified in ~30% of PD cases in some ethnicities.
source: Pathogenic mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) account for ~1% of all PD cases, of which LRRK2 G2019S is the most frequent; identified in ~30% of cases in some ethnicities (Ozelius et al., 2006; Hulihan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Affected LRRK2 individuals develop a late-onset, L-DOPA-responsive motor parkinsonism.
source: Affected LRRK2 individuals develop a late-onset, L-DOPA-responsive motor parkinsonism that is clinically and often pathologically indistinguishable from idiopathic PD (Haugland, 2002; Gaig et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: LRRK2-associated parkinsonism is clinically and often pathologically indistinguishable from idiopathic PD.
source: Affected LRRK2 individuals develop a late-onset, L-DOPA-responsive motor parkinsonism that is clinically and often pathologically indistinguishable from idiopathic PD (Haugland, 2002; Gaig et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Dopamine PET imaging of affected LRRK2 mutation carriers reveals progressive neurochemical alterations similar to those of sporadic PD, namely impaired presynaptic dopamine function.
source: Dopamine PET imaging of affected LRRK2 mutation carriers reveals progressive neurochemical alterations similar to those of sporadic PD, namely impaired presynaptic dopamine function (Adams et al., 2005; Nandhagopal et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Clinically asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers show early increases in dopamine turnover by PET.
source: Further study in LRRK2 families reveals surprising alterations in clinically asymptomatic, otherwise healthy, mutation carriers, including: (i) early increases in dopamine turnover by PET (Sossi et al., 2010), (ii) changes in cortical connectivity by resting state MRI and neurochemical changes (Adams et al., 2005; Helmich et al., 2015; Vilas et al., 2015), and (iii) alterations in cognitive tests of executive function (Thaler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sossi et al., 2010.

claim: Clinically asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers show changes in cortical connectivity by resting state MRI.
source: Further study in LRRK2 families reveals surprising alterations in clinically asymptomatic, otherwise healthy, mutation carriers, including: (i) early increases in dopamine turnover by PET (Sossi et al., 2010), (ii) changes in cortical connectivity by resting state MRI and neurochemical changes (Adams et al., 2005; Helmich et al., 2015; Vilas et al., 2015), and (iii) alterations in cognitive tests of executive function (Thaler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Clinically asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers show neurochemical changes.
source: Further study in LRRK2 families reveals surprising alterations in clinically asymptomatic, otherwise healthy, mutation carriers, including: (i) early increases in dopamine turnover by PET (Sossi et al., 2010), (ii) changes in cortical connectivity by resting state MRI and neurochemical changes (Adams et al., 2005; Helmich et al., 2015; Vilas et al., 2015), and (iii) alterations in cognitive tests of executive function (Thaler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Clinically asymptomatic LRRK2 mutation carriers show alterations in cognitive tests of executive function.
source: Further study in LRRK2 families reveals surprising alterations in clinically asymptomatic, otherwise healthy, mutation carriers, including: (i) early increases in dopamine turnover by PET (Sossi et al., 2010), (ii) changes in cortical connectivity by resting state MRI and neurochemical changes (Adams et al., 2005; Helmich et al., 2015; Vilas et al., 2015), and (iii) alterations in cognitive tests of executive function (Thaler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Thaler et al., 2013.

claim: Cell death and overt motor dysfunction are late occurrences in PD, preceded by dysfunction of dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic systems.
source: Advances in our understanding of PD argue cell death and overt motor dysfunction are late occurrences, preceded by dysfunction of dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about PD progression.

claim: In model systems modelling PD etiology, the underlying pathophysiology and phenotypes should be expected to be initially subtle, progressive, and include dysfunction of multiple neuronal systems, prior to cell loss.
source: In this light, in model systems modelling PD etiology, the underlying pathophysiology and phenotypes should also be expected to be initially subtle, progressive, and include dysfunction of multiple neuronal systems, prior to cell loss.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what to expect in animal models based on understanding of human PD progression.

claim: The LRRK2 G2019S substitution was engineered into the endogenous mouse gene to create G2019S knock-in mice (GKI).
source: We engineered the LRRK2 G2019S substitution into the endogenous mouse gene (G2019S knock-in mice; GKI) which produced reductions in basal and pharmacologically evoked nigrostriatal dopamine release in vivo in mice aged >12 months by microdialysis (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the generation of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: GKI mice aged >12 months show reductions in basal and pharmacologically evoked nigrostriatal dopamine release in vivo by microdialysis.
source: We engineered the LRRK2 G2019S substitution into the endogenous mouse gene (G2019S knock-in mice; GKI) which produced reductions in basal and pharmacologically evoked nigrostriatal dopamine release in vivo in mice aged >12 months by microdialysis (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: The Parkinson's-like deficit in dopamine release in GKI mice was not observed at 6 months.
source: This Parkinson's-like deficit was not observed at 6 months, and occurred despite a normal compliment of nigral neurons and nigrostriatal dopamine markers (TH).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: The Parkinson's-like deficit in dopamine release in aged GKI mice occurred despite a normal compliment of nigral neurons and nigrostriatal dopamine markers (TH).
source: This Parkinson's-like deficit was not observed at 6 months, and occurred despite a normal compliment of nigral neurons and nigrostriatal dopamine markers (TH).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: In cortical neurons cultured from GKI mice, increases in glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic transmission were observed at 21 days in vitro.
source: Contrastingly, in cortical neurons cultured from the same GKI mice, we observed increases in glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic transmission at 21 days in vitro (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Beccano-Kelly et al., 2014.

claim: Young GKI animals exhibit increased exploratory rearing behavior.
source: Young animals exhibit increased exploratory rearing behavior and increases in striatal glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing increased rearing in young GKI mice.

claim: Young GKI animals exhibit increases in striatal glutamate transmission.
source: Young animals exhibit increased exploratory rearing behavior and increases in striatal glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2 showing increased sEPSC frequency.

claim: Young GKI animals exhibit increases in striatal dopamine transmission.
source: Young animals exhibit increased exploratory rearing behavior and increases in striatal glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3 showing altered dopamine release dynamics.

claim: As GKI mice age, they exhibit less exploratory rearing.
source: As GKI mice age, they exhibit less exploratory rearing and reductions in both glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing age-dependent decline in rearing.

claim: As GKI mice age, they exhibit reductions in glutamate transmission.
source: As GKI mice age, they exhibit less exploratory rearing and reductions in both glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2 showing age-dependent decline in sEPSC frequency.

claim: As GKI mice age, they exhibit reductions in dopamine transmission.
source: As GKI mice age, they exhibit less exploratory rearing and reductions in both glutamate and dopamine transmission.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3 and prior microdialysis data showing age-dependent changes.

claim: Extracellular lifetime of single dopamine release events is enhanced in young GKI animals.
source: However, extracellular lifetime of single dopamine release events is enhanced in young GKI animals and maintained in aged animals, at which point wild-type littermate values have increased to parity.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3B showing increased decay times in young GKI mice.

claim: Extracellular lifetime of single dopamine release events is maintained in aged GKI animals.
source: However, extracellular lifetime of single dopamine release events is enhanced in young GKI animals and maintained in aged animals, at which point wild-type littermate values have increased to parity.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3B showing persistent increased decay times in aged GKI mice.

claim: Wild-type littermate dopamine transient decay times increase with age to reach parity with GKI values.
source: However, extracellular lifetime of single dopamine release events is enhanced in young GKI animals and maintained in aged animals, at which point wild-type littermate values have increased to parity.
evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data in Figure 3B showing age-dependent increases in WT decay times.

claim: The LRRK2 G2019S mutation produces alterations in young adult mice, most of which decline with age.
source: Several measures demonstrate that the LRRK2 G2019S mutation produces alterations in young adult mice, most of which decline with age, prior to ages where hypodopaminergia, mitochondrial and tau pathology are observed.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Alterations in young GKI mice decline prior to ages where hypodopaminergia, mitochondrial and tau pathology are observed.
source: Several measures demonstrate that the LRRK2 G2019S mutation produces alterations in young adult mice, most of which decline with age, prior to ages where hypodopaminergia, mitochondrial and tau pathology are observed.
evidence: This is based on the current findings and prior observations about when pathology appears in these mice.

claim: Understanding the early pathophysiological changes in etiological models may offer the best hope for development of neuroprotection in PD and related diseases.
source: We conclude that understanding the early pathophysiological changes in etiological models may offer the best hope for development of neuroprotection in PD and related diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: Longo et al. (2014) reported that a similar line of homozygous GKI mice weighed significantly less (~15%) than littermates.
source: Recently, Longo et al. (2014) reported that a similar line of homozygous GKI mice weighed significantly less (~15%) than littermates (Longo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study.

claim: No reductions in weight were detected in the founding GKI colony at Mayo Clinic, Florida.
source: We did not detect genotype-dependent weight alterations in our founding colony at Mayo Clinic, Florida (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: No reductions in weight were found in comparisons of multiple litters in the UBC colony over a wide range of ages.
source: Here, we found no reductions in weight in comparisons of multiple litters in the UBC colony, over a wide range of ages (Figure 1A. total animals WT n = 171, GKI heterozygous n = 276 mice and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1. GKI homozygous n = 162).
evidence: This is supported by weight data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GKI mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates in weight for up to 500 days.
source: Conversely, while GKI mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates for up to 500 days, a significant genotype-age interaction was detected due to small but significant increases in mean weight of both heterozygous and homozygous GKI animals at 500–600 days (Figure 1A.; 2-way ANOVA, genotype F(2,588)=1.8, p=0.17, interaction F(12,588)=1.7, p=0.049, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by weight data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 1A.

claim: A significant genotype-age interaction was detected in GKI mouse weight due to small but significant increases in mean weight of both heterozygous and homozygous GKI animals at 500–600 days.
source: Conversely, while GKI mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates for up to 500 days, a significant genotype-age interaction was detected due to small but significant increases in mean weight of both heterozygous and homozygous GKI animals at 500–600 days (Figure 1A.; 2-way ANOVA, genotype F(2,588)=1.8, p=0.17, interaction F(12,588)=1.7, p=0.049, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by weight data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LRRK2 G2019S parkinsonism is inherited as a Mendelian dominant condition and manifests in heterozygous carriers.
source: LRRK2 G2019S parkinsonism is inherited as a Mendelian dominant condition and manifests in heterozygous carriers (Trinh et al., 2014; Kachergus et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Striatal dopamine levels were normal by microdialysis in GKI mice at 1–6 months.
source: Based on our previous results (Yue et al., 2015) we chose to examine two life stages; early ages when striatal dopamine levels were previously normal by microdialysis (1–6 months;<6 m) and an aged time point when striatal dialysate dopamine levels were reduced (12–18 months;>12), but prior to detection of mitochondrial abnormalities (observed at >22 months [Yue et al., 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: Striatal dialysate dopamine levels were reduced in GKI mice at 12–18 months.
source: Based on our previous results (Yue et al., 2015) we chose to examine two life stages; early ages when striatal dopamine levels were previously normal by microdialysis (1–6 months;<6 m) and an aged time point when striatal dialysate dopamine levels were reduced (12–18 months;>12), but prior to detection of mitochondrial abnormalities (observed at >22 months [Yue et al., 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondrial abnormalities in GKI mice were observed at >22 months.
source: Based on our previous results (Yue et al., 2015) we chose to examine two life stages; early ages when striatal dopamine levels were previously normal by microdialysis (1–6 months;<6 m) and an aged time point when striatal dialysate dopamine levels were reduced (12–18 months;>12), but prior to detection of mitochondrial abnormalities (observed at >22 months [Yue et al., 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: There was no main effect of genotype upon mouse weight (2-way ANOVA, genotype F(2,588)=1.8, p=0.17).
source: Conversely, while GKI mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates for up to 500 days, a significant genotype-age interaction was detected due to small but significant increases in mean weight of both heterozygous and homozygous GKI animals at 500–600 days (Figure 1A.; 2-way ANOVA, genotype F(2,588)=1.8, p=0.17, interaction F(12,588)=1.7, p=0.049, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the weight analysis.

claim: There was a significant interaction between weight and age in GKI mice (2-way ANOVA, interaction F(12,588)=1.7, p=0.049).
source: Conversely, while GKI mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates for up to 500 days, a significant genotype-age interaction was detected due to small but significant increases in mean weight of both heterozygous and homozygous GKI animals at 500–600 days (Figure 1A.; 2-way ANOVA, genotype F(2,588)=1.8, p=0.17, interaction F(12,588)=1.7, p=0.049, and see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the weight analysis.

claim: In the oldest age group (500-600 days), there was a statistically significant increase in GKI mean weight (post-test p=0.018).
source: Weights were not significantly different at any age up to 500 days (i; animal n shown in ii); however, in the oldest age group there was a statistically significant increase in GKI mean weight (post-test *p=0.018).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the weight analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Longo et al. (2014) found homozygous GKI mice exhibited hyperactivity at all ages tested.
source: Longo et al. (2014) found homozygous GKI mice exhibited hyperactivity at all ages tested (Longo et al., 2014); although such a result might be impacted by lower body weight in mutants.
evidence: This statement references findings from another study.

claim: An increase (~10%) in open field activity was previously observed in a small cohort of homozygous GKI mice at 6 (but not 12) months in the founding colony.
source: In agreement, we previously observed an increase (~10%) in open field activity in a small cohort of homozygous GKI mice at 6 (but not 12) months in the founding colony (Yue et al., 2015); whereas hyperactivity was not observed at any age in heterozygous mice (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: Hyperactivity was not observed at any age in heterozygous GKI mice in the founding colony.
source: In agreement, we previously observed an increase (~10%) in open field activity in a small cohort of homozygous GKI mice at 6 (but not 12) months in the founding colony (Yue et al., 2015); whereas hyperactivity was not observed at any age in heterozygous mice (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: No significant effects of genotype or age were found on open field exploration in large cohorts of heterozygous GKI mice (2-way ANOVA: F(1,212)=0.09, 0.002, 0.007 and p=0.8, 0.9 and 0.9 for age, genotype and interaction, respectively).
source: Here we tested large cohorts in the open field exploration task and, in agreement with our previous report, found no significant effects (Figure 1B.i, WT n = 66 and 34, GKI n = 72 and 44, for <6 and >12 months, respectively; 2-way ANOVA: F(1,212)=0.09, 0.002, 0.007 and p=0.8, 0.9 and 0.9 for age, genotype and interaction, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the open field behavior analysis shown in Figure 1B.i.

claim: No evidence for thigmotaxis was found at either age point in GKI mice, suggesting a lack of anxiety- or anxiolytic-like phenotypes.
source: We similarly found no evidence for thigmotaxis at either age point, suggesting a lack of anxiety- or anxiolytic-like phenotypes, which may have altered open field exploration (center path ratios were not significantly different).
evidence: This is based on analysis of center path ratios in the open field test.

claim: In the cylinder exploration test, significant age and age-genotype interaction effects were found (2-way ANOVA: F(1,187)=23.6, 7.3, and p=0.0001, 0.008 for age and genotype-age interaction, respectively).
source: Contrastingly, in the cylinder exploration test conducted in a smaller environment that may stimulate mice or relieve some stress of open field testing, we found significant age and age-genotype interaction effects (Figure 1B.ii, WT n = 50 and 33, GKI n = 59 and 49, for <6 and >12 months, respectively; 2-way ANOVA: F(1,187)=23.6, 7.3, and p=0.0001, 0.008 for age and genotype-age interaction, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cylinder test analysis shown in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: GKI mice aged <6 months exhibited a significant ~25% increase in rearing events relative to WT littermates (p=0.009).
source: Post-test analysis demonstrated a significant ~25% increase in rearing events in GKI mice aged <6 m, relative to WT littermates (p=0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cylinder test analysis shown in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: Rearing events in GKI mice were significantly reduced with age (p=0.0001).
source: This phenomenon was significantly reduced with age in GKI mice (p=0.0001) but not WT animals (p=0.3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cylinder test analysis shown in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: Rearing events in WT animals were not significantly reduced with age (p=0.3).
source: This phenomenon was significantly reduced with age in GKI mice (p=0.0001) but not WT animals (p=0.3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cylinder test analysis shown in Figure 1B.ii.

claim: The G2019S mutation (at disease-relevant heterozygous physiological expression levels) results in alterations to behavior in young adult mice, independent of changes to animal weight.
source: Together, the behavioral data demonstrate that the G2019S mutation (at disease-relevant heterozygous physiological expression levels) results in alterations to behavior in young adult mice, independent of changes to animal weight.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral and weight data presented.

claim: In GKI mice, increased exploratory rearing likely reflects altered motivation for exploration, rather than motor function per se.
source: Here, in GKI mice, this manifested as early increases in exploratory rearing without changes in open field exploration and thus likely reflects altered motivation for exploration, rather than motor function per se.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing context-dependent changes.

claim: GKI mice have a propensity to exhibit hyperactivity, but one that is context dependent.
source: We conclude, in broad agreement with previous reports (Yue et al., 2015; Longo et al., 2014), that GKI mice have a propensity to exhibit hyperactivity, but one that is context dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current behavioral data and prior reports.

claim: Glutamate release is augmented in networks of cultured GKI cortical neurons, as demonstrated by a > 35% increase in miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency at 3 weeks in vitro.
source: Glutamate release is augmented in networks of cultured GKI cortical neurons, as demonstrated by a > 35% increase in miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency at 3 weeks in vitro (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Beccano-Kelly et al., 2014.

claim: Intrinsic membrane properties of SPNs are not altered by the presence of G2019S LRRK2.
source: Intrinsic membrane properties were as predicted for SPNs (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2015; Milnerwood et al., 2013; Milnerwood et al., 2010) and, although there were statistically significant age effects upon membrane capacitance (Cm), membrane resistance (Rm) and decay time constants (Tau m), there were no genotype or genotype-age interaction effects (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1; 2-way ANOVA values included). Thus, intrinsic membrane properties of SPNs are not altered by the presence of G2019S LRRK2.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age upon mean sEPSC amplitude (2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=3.92, p=0.049).
source: Analysis of spontaneous EPSCs (sEPSCs, Figure 2A) revealed a significant main age effect upon event amplitude (Figure 2A.i. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=3.92, p=0.049, WT n = 40(17) and 31(12), GKI n = 53(20) and 44(15), for 1–3 and >12 months, respectively), but no genotype or genotype-age interaction effects (F(1,165)=2.1, 1.8, p=0.15 and 0.18, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no genotype or genotype-age interaction effect on sEPSC amplitude (F(1,165)=2.1, 1.8, p=0.15 and 0.18, respectively).
source: Analysis of spontaneous EPSCs (sEPSCs, Figure 2A) revealed a significant main age effect upon event amplitude (Figure 2A.i. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=3.92, p=0.049, WT n = 40(17) and 31(12), GKI n = 53(20) and 44(15), for 1–3 and >12 months, respectively), but no genotype or genotype-age interaction effects (F(1,165)=2.1, 1.8, p=0.15 and 0.18, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Analysis of sEPSC frequencies revealed significant main genotype and age effects (2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=6.3, 17.3, p=0.013, 0.0001, respectively).
source: Contrastingly, analysis of sEPSC frequencies revealed significant main genotype and age effects (Figure 2A.ii. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=6.3, 17.3, p=0.013, 0.0001, respectively), and a significant interaction between genotype and age (F(1,165)=7.8, p=0.006).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant interaction between genotype and age on sEPSC frequency (F(1,165)=7.8, p=0.006).
source: Contrastingly, analysis of sEPSC frequencies revealed significant main genotype and age effects (Figure 2A.ii. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,165)=6.3, 17.3, p=0.013, 0.0001, respectively), and a significant interaction between genotype and age (F(1,165)=7.8, p=0.006).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GKI SPNs aged 1–3 months exhibited a significant ~47% increase in sEPSC frequency relative to WT littermates (p=0.0004).
source: Post-tests demonstrated a significant ~47% increase in sEPSC frequency in GKI SPNs aged 1–3 months, relative to WT littermates (p=0.0004).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: sEPSC frequency was significantly reduced with age in GKI mice (p=0.0001).
source: This phenomenon was significantly reduced with age in GKI mice (p=0.0001), but not WT animals (p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: sEPSC frequency was not significantly reduced with age in WT animals (p=0.6).
source: This phenomenon was significantly reduced with age in GKI mice (p=0.0001), but not WT animals (p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Inter-event interval cumulative probabilities demonstrated that sEPSC frequency is higher in GKI SPNs at 1 and 3, but not 12 or 18 months of age.
source: To more discretely interrogate the age-dependency of this large increase in sEPSC event frequency, comparisons were made between GKI and WT data sets in approximate 1, 3, 12 and 18 month groupings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, RM-ANOVA values included); inter-event interval cumulative probabilities demonstrated that frequency is higher in GKI SPNs at 1 and 3, but not 12 or 18 months of age.
evidence: This is based on analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) found a similar increase in SPN event frequency in slices from similar GKI mice (aged < 1 month).
source: A recent report by Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) also found a similar increase in SPN event frequency in slices from similar GKI mice (aged < 1 month) (Matikainen-Ankney et al., 2016), which was concluded to be predominantly due to action potential-mediated transmission (only a strong trend toward increased frequency was observed in the presence TTX).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study.

claim: Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) concluded that increased SPN event frequency in GKI mice was predominantly due to action potential-mediated transmission.
source: A recent report by Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) also found a similar increase in SPN event frequency in slices from similar GKI mice (aged < 1 month) (Matikainen-Ankney et al., 2016), which was concluded to be predominantly due to action potential-mediated transmission (only a strong trend toward increased frequency was observed in the presence TTX).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study.

claim: sEPSCs in the coronal slice preparation used in this study are TTX-insensitive, and thus predominantly miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs).
source: We have previously demonstrated that sEPSCs in our coronal slice preparation are TTX-insensitive, and thus predominantly miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) (Milnerwood et al., 2010); however, the possibility remains that an increase in basal GKI event frequency is due to anomalous preservation of action potential-dependent release.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Milnerwood et al., 2010.

claim: GKI event amplitudes and frequencies were insensitive to TTX application.
source: We found that GKI event amplitudes and frequencies were insensitive to TTX application (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), with only a weak trend toward increased (not reduced) frequency following blockade of action potential firing.
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: sEPSCs in GKI slices are predominantly, if not entirely, independent of action potentials and therefore represent miniature release.
source: We conclude that sEPSCs in GKI slices are predominantly, if not entirely, independent of action potentials and therefore represent miniature release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TTX experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No significant genotype effect was found upon postsynaptic dendritic spine-like structures (quantified from Golgi impregnation).
source: A simple explanation for increased glutamatergic event frequency is an increase in the number of synapses (with equal release probability); however, we found no significant genotype effect upon postsynaptic dendritic spine-like structures (quantified from Golgi impregnation), or immunohistochemical staining of presynaptic vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2 (VGluT1, VGluT2; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: No significant genotype effect was found upon immunohistochemical staining of presynaptic vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2 (VGluT1, VGluT2).
source: A simple explanation for increased glutamatergic event frequency is an increase in the number of synapses (with equal release probability); however, we found no significant genotype effect upon postsynaptic dendritic spine-like structures (quantified from Golgi impregnation), or immunohistochemical staining of presynaptic vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2 (VGluT1, VGluT2; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: GKI SPNs in slices from young mice exhibited no difference in sEPSC event amplitude but significant increases in event frequency in the absence of changes to synapse numbers.
source: Thus, similarly to glutamatergic mEPSCs in cortical cultures at 3 weeks in vitro (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2014), GKI SPNs in slices from young mice exhibited no difference in sEPSC event amplitude but significant increases in event frequency in the absence of changes to synapse numbers.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the electrophysiology and morphology data.

claim: Early increases in glutamate release frequency in GKI SPNs are not maintained in SPNs of slices from older animals.
source: These specific early increases in glutamate release frequency (as opposed to event amplitude) are not maintained in SPNs of slices from older animals; in agreement with Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) who also report no changes to synapse density (Matikainen-Ankney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the age-dependent data and agreement with another study.

claim: Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) report no changes to synapse density in GKI mice.
source: These specific early increases in glutamate release frequency (as opposed to event amplitude) are not maintained in SPNs of slices from older animals; in agreement with Matikainen-Ankney et al. (2016) who also report no changes to synapse density (Matikainen-Ankney et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study.

claim: There was a significant effect of age, but no significant genotype effect upon AMPA:NMDA ratios of GKI and WT eEPSCs (2-way ANOVA; F(1,106)=4.3, 0.002, p=0.041, 0.97 for age and genotype, respectively).
source: Although there was a significant effect of age, we found no significant genotype effect upon AMPA:NMDA ratios of GKI and WT eEPSCs (Figure 2B, 2-way ANOVA; F(1,106)=4.3, 0.002, p=0.041, 0.97 for age and genotype, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the eEPSC analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios were not significantly altered by genotype in slices from young mice (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47).
source: Paired-pulse ratios (often seen as indicative of presynaptic release probability) were not significantly altered by genotype in slices from young (Figure 2C.i and ii, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47) or aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the paired-pulse analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios were not significantly altered by genotype in slices from aged mice (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47).
source: Paired-pulse ratios (often seen as indicative of presynaptic release probability) were not significantly altered by genotype in slices from young (Figure 2C.i and ii, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47) or aged mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,96)=0.51, p=0.47).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the paired-pulse analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Several reports demonstrate a disconnection between alterations in miniature event frequency and predicted changes to PPRs.
source: Several reports demonstrate a disconnection between alterations in miniature event frequency and predicted changes to PPRs (Milnerwood et al., 2013; Cepeda et al., 2008; Sara et al., 2005; Ramirez et al., 2012; Crawford and Kavalali, 2015; Milnerwood and Raymond, 2007; Parisiadou et al., 2014; Mei et al., 2016; Akopian and Walsh, 2007) and recent evidence suggests the mechanisms for miniature and synchronous release may be distinct (reviewed in [Crawford and Kavalali, 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Recent evidence suggests the mechanisms for miniature and synchronous release may be distinct.
source: Several reports demonstrate a disconnection between alterations in miniature event frequency and predicted changes to PPRs (Milnerwood et al., 2013; Cepeda et al., 2008; Sara et al., 2005; Ramirez et al., 2012; Crawford and Kavalali, 2015; Milnerwood and Raymond, 2007; Parisiadou et al., 2014; Mei et al., 2016; Akopian and Walsh, 2007) and recent evidence suggests the mechanisms for miniature and synchronous release may be distinct (reviewed in [Crawford and Kavalali, 2015]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Specific alterations to spontaneous release may entirely underlie the increase observed in GKI slices.
source: Therefore, specific alterations to spontaneous release may entirely underlie the increase observed in GKI slices.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the literature about distinct release mechanisms.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation ratios are reduced (and release probability is increased) in thalamostriatal, relative to corticostriatal, terminals.
source: Alternatively, paired-pulse facilitation ratios are reduced (and release probability is increased) in thalamostriatal, relative to corticostriatal, terminals (Ding et al., 2008; Sciamanna et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Altered contributions of corticostriatal or thalamostriatal pathways might account for observed differences in young (and potentially masked differences in old) GKI slices.
source: Thus, altered contributions of one or both pathways might account for observed differences in young (and potentially masked differences in old) GKI slices.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about potential pathway-specific effects.

claim: Upon intrastriatal stimulation, glutamatergic terminals (and, by inference, PPRs) are subject to modulation by the simultaneous release of dopamine.
source: Upon intrastriatal stimulation, glutamatergic terminals (and, by inference, PPRs) are subject to modulation by the simultaneous release of dopamine (Bamford et al., 2004), among other transmitters.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bamford et al., 2004.

claim: In slices from LRRK2 overexpressing mice, PPR alterations were dependent upon the activity of presynaptic D2 receptors.
source: In slices from LRRK2 overexpressing mice, we found PPR alterations were dependent upon the activity of presynaptic D2 receptors (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Beccano-Kelly et al., 2015.

claim: In the presence of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (10 uM), there was a significant main effect of genotype upon PPRs; GKI currents were reduced relative to WT controls (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,17)=4.8, p=0.042).
source: Here, in the presence of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (Q; 10 uM, bath applied) we found a significant main effect of genotype upon PPRs; GKI currents were reduced relative to WT controls (Figure 2C.iii, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,17)=4.8, p=0.042), indicative of a relatively higher initial release probability at GKI synapses, when D2 receptors were stimulated in both genotypes.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the quinpirole experiment shown in Figure 2C.iii.

claim: Reduced GKI PPRs in the presence of quinpirole are indicative of a relatively higher initial release probability at GKI synapses, when D2 receptors were stimulated in both genotypes.
source: Here, in the presence of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (Q; 10 uM, bath applied) we found a significant main effect of genotype upon PPRs; GKI currents were reduced relative to WT controls (Figure 2C.iii, 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,17)=4.8, p=0.042), indicative of a relatively higher initial release probability at GKI synapses, when D2 receptors were stimulated in both genotypes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PPR data in the presence of quinpirole.

claim: Quinpirole increased WT PPRs (2-way RM-ANOVA treatment F(1,32)=7.5, p=0.01 before vs. after quinpirole).
source: This difference is likely due to D2 agonism having increased WT PPRs in this subset of cells (n = 9 (3); 2-way RM-ANOVA treatment F(1,32)=7.5, p=0.01 before vs. after quinpirole), by presynaptic D2 negative tuning of initial release probability (and resultantly increased PPR) (Beccano-Kelly et al., 2015; Bamford et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the quinpirole experiment.

claim: Quinpirole had no effect on PPR in GKI slices.
source: Conversely, quinpirole had no effect on PPR in GKI (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that D2 negative tuning upon presynaptic terminals is dysfunctional, or saturated, at GKI synapses.
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: D2 negative tuning upon presynaptic terminals is dysfunctional, or saturated, at GKI synapses.
source: Conversely, quinpirole had no effect on PPR in GKI (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that D2 negative tuning upon presynaptic terminals is dysfunctional, or saturated, at GKI synapses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quinpirole data in GKI slices.

claim: The D2 antagonist remoxipride (10 uM) had no significant effect upon GKI PPRs.
source: The D2 antagonist remoxipride (10 uM, bath applied) also had no significant effect upon GKI PPRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 5); suggesting that acute D2 activation on glutamatergic terminals is dysfunctional, not saturated.
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Acute D2 activation on glutamatergic terminals is dysfunctional, not saturated, in GKI mice.
source: The D2 antagonist remoxipride (10 uM, bath applied) also had no significant effect upon GKI PPRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 5); suggesting that acute D2 activation on glutamatergic terminals is dysfunctional, not saturated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the remoxipride data.

claim: Loss of dopamine-dependent negative regulation may contribute to basal increases in GKI event frequency at young age.
source: This loss of dopamine-dependent negative regulation may contribute to basal increases in GKI event frequency at this young age, if intrinsic differences in glutamate release are beyond modulation by this form of negative regulation (Bamford et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the mechanism underlying increased event frequency.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios were initially shown to be elevated in direct pathway SPNs.
source: SPNs are equally subdivided by postsynaptic D1 or D2 dopamine receptor expression and form the direct and indirect striatal output pathways, respectively. Paired-pulse ratios were initially shown to be elevated in direct pathway SPNs (Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007), and although subsequent reports found no difference in PPRs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2008), miniature EPSC frequencies appear consistently higher in D2 indirect pathway SPNs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007.

claim: Subsequent reports found no difference in PPRs between D1 and D2 SPNs.
source: SPNs are equally subdivided by postsynaptic D1 or D2 dopamine receptor expression and form the direct and indirect striatal output pathways, respectively. Paired-pulse ratios were initially shown to be elevated in direct pathway SPNs (Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007), and although subsequent reports found no difference in PPRs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2008), miniature EPSC frequencies appear consistently higher in D2 indirect pathway SPNs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cepeda et al., 2008 and Ding et al., 2008.

claim: Miniature EPSC frequencies appear consistently higher in D2 indirect pathway SPNs.
source: SPNs are equally subdivided by postsynaptic D1 or D2 dopamine receptor expression and form the direct and indirect striatal output pathways, respectively. Paired-pulse ratios were initially shown to be elevated in direct pathway SPNs (Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007), and although subsequent reports found no difference in PPRs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2008), miniature EPSC frequencies appear consistently higher in D2 indirect pathway SPNs (Cepeda et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cepeda et al., 2008 and Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007.

claim: No cell-type or age-effect was found on sEPSC event frequencies of D1 or D2 SPNs in slices from GKI mice (2-way ANOVA; F(1,19)=1.23, 0.56, p=0.21, 0.46 for cell type and age, respectively).
source: We found no cell-type or age-effect on sEPSC event frequencies of D1 or D2 SPNs in slices from GKI mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, 2-way ANOVA; F(1,19)=1.23, 0.56, p=0.21, 0.46 for cell type and age, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the D1/D2 cell-type analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Quinpirole application did not have a consistent effect upon eEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse ratios in either D1 or D2 SPNs from GKI mice.
source: We also found that quinpirole application did not have a consistent effect upon eEPSC amplitude or paired-pulse ratios in either D1 or D2 SPNs from GKI mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Remoxipride had no effect upon event amplitude or frequency in GKI SPNs.
source: Similarly, remoxipride had no effect upon event amplitude or frequency in GKI SPNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is based on data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Presynaptic glutamate transmission onto SPNs of GKI mice is augmented (due to altered release, not changes in synapse number) at an early age when presynaptic D2 tuning is also dysfunctional.
source: Together the data suggest that presynaptic glutamate transmission onto SPNs of GKI mice is augmented (due to altered release, not changes in synapse number) at an early age when presynaptic D2 tuning is also dysfunctional.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the glutamate transmission data.

claim: Initial levels of glutamate activity in GKI SPNs decline over the animals' lifetime, unlike WT SPNs.
source: These initial levels of activity decline over the animals' lifetime, unlike WT SPNs.
evidence: This is a summary of the age-dependent findings in glutamate transmission.

claim: A significant reduction in basal extracellular dopamine levels was previously found in GKI mice aged 12, but not 6 months.
source: We previously found a significant reduction in basal extracellular dopamine levels in GKI mice aged 12, but not 6 months (Yue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2015.

claim: Reduced extracellular dopamine in old GKI animals was interpreted as a latent impairment of dopamine release.
source: As no differences in the total amount of dopamine were detected, reduced extracellular dopamine in old animals was interpreted as a latent impairment of dopamine release.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior findings from Yue et al., 2015.

claim: There was no effect of genotype on single pulse evoked dopamine release peak currents and calibrated extracellular dopamine peak concentrations in slices from young GKI and WT animals (2-way ANOVA; F(1,140)=0.001, p=0.97).
source: Single pulses evoking dopamine release by increasing stimulus intensities (50 - ~450 uA, 0.01 Hz) revealed similar peak currents and calibrated extracellular dopamine peak concentrations in slices from young GKI and WT animals; there was no effect of genotype (Figure 3A.i and ii. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,140)=0.001, p=0.97).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the voltammetry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Single pulse evoked dopamine release declined by approximately 50% in aged animals.
source: Single pulse evoked dopamine release had declined by approximately 50% in aged animals, (Figure 3A.ii), but again there was no effect of genotype (2-way ANOVA; F(1,141)=1.79, p=0.18).
evidence: This is based on voltammetry data shown in Figure 3A.ii.

claim: There was no effect of genotype on single pulse evoked dopamine release in aged animals (2-way ANOVA; F(1,141)=1.79, p=0.18).
source: Single pulse evoked dopamine release had declined by approximately 50% in aged animals, (Figure 3A.ii), but again there was no effect of genotype (2-way ANOVA; F(1,141)=1.79, p=0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the voltammetry analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is no basal impairment to stimulated dopamine release in aged GKI mice, despite reduced extracellular dopamine in vivo.
source: The data suggest there is no basal impairment to stimulated dopamine release in aged GKI mice, despite reduced extracellular dopamine in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the voltammetry data and prior in vivo findings.

claim: Over 10 min of repeated stimulation in slices from young animals, there was a significant main effect of genotype (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,53)=8.5, p=0.005).
source: Over 10 min, in slices from young animals, we found a significant main effect of genotype (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,53)=8.5, p=0.005), and a significant interaction between genotype and pulse number (F(4,212)=4.0, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the repeated stimulation experiment shown in Figure 3A.ii.

claim: Over 10 min of repeated stimulation in slices from young animals, there was a significant interaction between genotype and pulse number (F(4,212)=4.0, p=0.003).
source: Over 10 min, in slices from young animals, we found a significant main effect of genotype (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,53)=8.5, p=0.005), and a significant interaction between genotype and pulse number (F(4,212)=4.0, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the repeated stimulation experiment shown in Figure 3A.ii.

claim: Where WT dopamine release amplitudes declined with repeated stimulation, responses in young GKI slices increased such that there was significantly more dopamine released.
source: Where WT amplitudes declined, responses in young GKI slices increased such that there was significantly more dopamine released (Figure 3A.ii).
evidence: This is based on voltammetry data shown in Figure 3A.ii.

claim: In slices from aged mice, neither genotype exhibited a relative increase or decrease in dopamine release over repeated stimulation (2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,61)=0.65, p=0.4).
source: Conversely, in slices from aged mice, neither genotype exhibited a relative increase or decrease in dopamine release over the same timeframe (Figure 3A.ii; 2-way RM-ANOVA; F(1,61)=0.65, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the repeated stimulation experiment shown in Figure 3A.ii.

claim: The GKI mutation results in alterations to the regulation of dopamine release in young animals, rather than disturbing the mechanics of single stimuli-evoked release.
source: The data suggest that the GKI mutation results in alterations to the regulation of dopamine release in young animals, rather than disturbing the mechanics of single stimuli-evoked release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the voltammetry data showing normal single-pulse but altered repeated-pulse responses.

claim: Alterations to dopamine release regulation in young GKI mice are no longer present at 12 months.
source: Furthermore, this alteration is no longer present at 12 months.
evidence: This is based on the age-dependent voltammetry data.

claim: There was a significant age-dependent increase in D2 autoreceptor mediated paired-pulse depression (post-test p=0.001).
source: Paired-pulses (Figure 3A.i and iii) evoked predicted depression of the second pulse in WT and GKI slices from young (~70%) and aged animals (~80%); there was a significant effect of age, but not genotype on paired-pulse ratios (Figure 3A.iii. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,77)=37.9, 0.142 p=0.0001 and 0.7, respectively; post-test 3 month vs. > 12 month p=0.0002 and 0.0002 for WT and GKI, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the paired-pulse analysis shown in Figure 3A.iii.

claim: There was no main effect of genotype on dopamine paired-pulse ratios (p=0.7).
source: Paired-pulses (Figure 3A.i and iii) evoked predicted depression of the second pulse in WT and GKI slices from young (~70%) and aged animals (~80%); there was a significant effect of age, but not genotype on paired-pulse ratios (Figure 3A.iii. 2-way ANOVA; F(1,77)=37.9, 0.142 p=0.0001 and 0.7, respectively; post-test 3 month vs. > 12 month p=0.0002 and 0.0002 for WT and GKI, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the paired-pulse analysis shown in Figure 3A.iii.

claim: D2 autoreceptor signaling and short-term negative regulation of dopamine release is not altered by the GKI mutation.
source: The data demonstrate that D2 autoreceptor signaling and short-term negative regulation of dopamine release is not altered by the GKI mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the paired-pulse data.

claim: In the initial presence of quinpirole (50 nM), response peaks of slices from mice aged 3 months were reduced by ~20% in both genotypes.
source: To investigate chronic D2 activation, we bath applied a low concentration of the D2 agonist quinpirole (50 nM, Figure 3B.i). In the initial presence of quinpirole (0 min; 10 min after switching perfusate), response peaks of slices from mice aged 3 months were reduced by ~20% in both genotypes.
evidence: This is based on voltammetry data shown in Figure 3B.i.
